text:
Maya Chen: heads-up — support just escalated a customer incident: short 30s spike led to a bunch of 429s and some 500s. They say billing shows no quota usage drop during the spike (odd). Can we treat this as a ratecap/burst policy repro?
Dan O'Reilly: link to support thread? want user id / org id to repro locally
Maya Chen: sent in DMs. Org: acme-payments, API key masked. timeline: 2026-03-14T14:06Z spike for ~25s, then normal. Reports show 429s and then a few 502s from the runtime.
Linus Patel: quick hypothesis: token-bucket burst allowance got consumed but metrics pipeline aggregator had a lag and billing sidecar didn't decrement in real time — support sees no quota change until ingestion window closed. But runtime should still reject after burst exhausted. Need concrete repro.
Priya Singh: customer attached logs — lots of: `error: 429 Rate limit exceeded; retry-after: 10` and `WARN kv-cache miss` right before 502s. They also saw a subsequent billing sync showing lot of requests credited after ~3m.
Alex Gomez: I can run a focused internal load test mimicking their spike shape: ramp to target quickly, hold for 20-30s, then drop. Would prefer to test both token-bucket config and leaky-window config to see classification.
Maya Chen: yes please. Our current global defaults are pretty permissive for bursts. We want to set sane defaults that avoid customer-facing 429s during short surges while protecting capacity. Also check if fallback routes triggered.
Dan O'Reilly: suggested test plan: 1) baseline steady-state RPM of 1000rpm; 2) spike shape: 0->2000rpm over 3s hold 25s drop; 3) vary burst window: 30s/60s and token bucket size. Record 429 rate, latency p95, and backend 5xx.
Linus Patel: make sure to capture per-route and per-org counters. Also enable detailed runtime traces for a small sample to see where requests are queued/dropped.
Alex Gomez: ok i'll run k6 with this scenario. Script snippet: ```js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { sleep } from 'k6';
export default function () {
  let res = http.get('https://api.redwood.test/v1/generate?org=acme-payments&key=TEST');
  sleep(0.05);
}
// run: k6 run --vus 400 --duration 30s spike.js
```
Priya Singh: include a run that uses short bursts of tiny concurrent requests (many tiny tokens) vs fewer bigger requests — helps tease apart token bucket vs concurrency limits.
Alex Gomez: results from first run (token-bucket default: burst_size=500 tokens, refill=100TPS): summary: total requests 12k, 429s: 18% (mostly during 5-30s), p95 latency jumped from 120ms -> 720ms during spike, backend 502s 0.6% immediately after spike.
Maya Chen: 18% 429s is too high for a short spike. What happened to the billing/usage discrepancy?
Linus Patel: I pulled metrics: quota-meter emitted token-consume events but host-level aggregator had a 90s ingestion delay under load; billing job reads aggregated counters after that window so support saw no immediate decrement. So billing UI lag is separate.
Dan O'Reilly: so two problems: 1) defaults allow a big initial burst but our refill can't keep up leading to sustained 429s during the spike tail; 2) metrics ingestion lag leads to billing confusion. We'll fix defaults and file a follow-up on metrics path.
Alex Gomez: I ran variant B with burst_size=250 tokens and refill same: 429s rose to 35% (worse). Variant C burst_size=800 tokens refill=200TPS: 429s drop to 4%, p95 spike 380ms, backend 502s negligible. But cost of bigger burst is headroom consumption — could enable for paid plans only.
Priya Singh: customers expect short spikes to succeed if they have reasonable baseline usage. Suggest default: burst_size = min(800, baseline_rpm * 0.2) and refill scaled to baseline. And make burst policy tiered: free-tier small, paid-tier larger.
Maya Chen: agree. Also add a safety cap to avoid cluster-wide overload: per-instance max-burst absolute cap (e.g., 1500 tokens).
Linus Patel: note: token semantics depend on request cost. For embeddings vs chat generation tokens differ. We should weight tokens by cost units rather than request count. In tests we used uniform small calls; need to rerun with heavier calls to ensure generator latency/kv cache pressure.
Alex Gomez: ran heavy-run with high-cost endpoint (streaming chat) using burst 800/refill200: 429s 3%, p95 1.2s during spike, memory pressure on runtime increased slightly and KV misses rose. Suggest pairing burst increases with recommended caching/batching config for high-cost endpoints.
Dan O'Reilly: actionable list: 1) update default burst heuristic to `min(800, baseline_rpm*0.2)` with absolute cap 1500; 2) make tier mapping docs and default for paid tiers higher; 3) add a billing-side flag to expose near-real-time 'pending consumption' during ingestion delay; 4) instrument ingestion lag alerts.
Maya Chen: who will pick which?
Linus Patel: I'll take ingestion lag alerts and metrics pipeline ticket.
Priya Singh: I will draft a short support FAQ explaining billing lag and what customers will see during spikes.
Alex Gomez: I'll open RFC for default burst heuristics and add e2e load test cases in our regression suite; will commit k6 scripts and baseline numbers to repo.
Dan O'Reilly: SRE oncall bot: `incident:create` — just kidding :) Seriously, can we schedule a 30m sync with platform/product to sign off on defaults?
Maya Chen: yes please — propose tomorrow 09:30 PST. I'll invite product + billing + support.
Alex Gomez: attaching raw logs summary and k6 output below for the ticket: ```
--- run: 2026-03-14 20:00Z spike-800-200
total: 12000
status_counts: {200: 9840, 429: 480, 502: 72, 500: 8}
latency_ms: {p50: 110, p95: 380, p99: 880}
```
Maya Chen: good thread. tagging action owners: @Linus @Alex @Priya. We'll follow up after the sync and update config in staging for a week before rolling.
SRE Oncall Bot: scheduled reminder: "Ratecap tuning sync" Tomorrow 09:30 PST — meeting created (link)
